story.title: Noah and the Midnight Respawn
story.subtitle: Eight levels through the strange, true science of sleep, cleared one eye-twitch at a time.

chapters.heading: Level 1: Server Maintenance at 2:14 A.M.
chapters.text:
Noah was three rounds into a losing streak, controller warm in his hands, when his phone buzzed on its own. Nobody had texted him.

The screen he'd never opened — some sleep app his mom installed and he'd muted on day one — lit up with a soft green moon. Then the moon blinked. Then it spoke, in a voice like an old game console booting up.

"USER DETECTED: AWAKE. AGAIN. LOADING OVERDUE BRIEFING."

Noah paused his match, which took actual willpower. "Did my phone just load a cutscene?"

The moon — it called itself **Circa** — unfolded into a full black-and-green terminal screen, text scrolling like a loading bar. "You have ignored me for one hundred and forty-one nights straight," it said. "Tonight, you walk the tutorial."

"Or," Noah said, "I finish my game."

"Your game will be here," Circa said. "You, statistically, will not be awake much longer either way. Your choice which you remember."

Noah looked at his dropping battery icon, then at the glowing moon. Curiosity won, the way it always did with him. He tapped the screen.

The floor of his bedroom dissolved into static, and the static turned into a hallway built out of loading bars.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Eye-Twitch Replay
chapters.text:
The hallway spat Noah into a dusty room that smelled like old cathode ray tubes. A projector flickered a black-and-white film on the wall: a sleeping boy, his eyelids twitching like a controller stick drifting on its own.

"Why's his face buffering?" Noah asked.

"In **1953**, two researchers named **Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman** watched exactly that," Circa said. "A sleeping boy's eyes flicking back and forth under closed lids. They called it **REM sleep** — rapid eye movement."

Noah leaned in, rewound the projector himself, and watched the flicker loop three times. "His brain's still running something. Like it never actually quit the game."

"Correct," Circa said. "During REM, the brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake. But your muscles go limp, so you physically can't act out whatever you're dreaming. Built-in anti-cheat, basically."

Noah snorted. "So my brain's still online, my body's just got no controller plugged in."

"Kleitman spent his whole career watching people sleep," Circa added. "People still call him the father of modern sleep research."

"Respect," Noah said. "One build, his whole career. I can't even stick with one game mode for a week."

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Ninety-Minute Respawn Timer
chapters.text:
The next room held a glowing graph, a wave rolling up and down like a heart monitor doing bicep curls. Noah traced one full loop with his finger, then another.

"This whole wave," Circa said, "repeats roughly every **ninety minutes**, all night long. You roll between quiet, deep non-REM sleep and that busy REM stage you just saw."

Noah counted the loops on the readout. "Four, five, six times a night? That's respawning on a timer whether you want to or not."

"Close enough," Circa said. "And the deepest dip in that wave — the real quiet stuff — is where your body dumps the most **growth hormone**. The stuff that actually makes a growing kid grow."

Noah glanced down at himself, unimpressed by his own height compared to half his grade. "So skipping sleep is basically skipping XP I could've used."

"You said it, not me," Circa said.

Noah pressed his palm flat against the glowing wave anyway, half a dare. It pulsed once under his hand, like it recognized the input, and the loop kept rolling on without him.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Clock Behind Your Eyes
chapters.text:
A narrow door led into a control room no bigger than a closet, cables running everywhere like the mess behind Noah's TV stand. One ticking light sat dead center, steady as a metronome.

"That," Circa said, "stands in for your **suprachiasmatic nucleus** — a pinhead of brain tissue sitting right where your eye nerves cross. It's your body's master clock."

Noah tapped the light. It ticked faster, almost nervous. "Master clock for what?"

"For knowing when to feel sleepy and when to feel awake. Scientists call that your **circadian rhythm** — from Latin words that just mean 'about a day.'"

"So it's basically a background process," Noah said. "Running whether I check it or not. Like my download queue."

"In **2017**, three scientists — **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** — won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the actual genes that keep that clock ticking."

Noah studied the tangle of wires, then rerouted one on instinct, the way he'd untangle a controller cord without thinking. The ticking light steadied into one calm, even rhythm.

"Nice patch," Circa said. "Most people never even open this menu."

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Night-Mode Vault
chapters.text:
Down another corridor sat a vault door, a single vial glowing faint blue inside the glass. Noah pressed his face close.

"That's **melatonin**," Circa said. "The hormone that tells your body it's bedtime. A scientist named **Aaron Lerner** and his team first isolated it in **1958**, pulling it out of a tiny gland in animal brains."

"So it's basically the game's night filter," Noah said. "Flips on, everything dims."

"Basically," Circa said.

The vault door slid open on its own, and a soft rinse of light swept the whole room, clearing away static Noah hadn't even noticed was there.

"What was that?"

"Your brain runs a nightly rinse cycle while you sleep," Circa said. "It flushes out waste, like clearing a cache. That same process is part of how your brain files today into long-term memory — that guitar chord you finally nailed yesterday, for instance."

Noah thought of the progression he'd been grinding on for a week, the one that had finally clicked that afternoon. "So sleep is basically how I save my progress."

"Exactly," Circa said. "No save, no keep."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Eleven-Day High Score
chapters.text:
The next room was a leaderboard, screens stacked floor to ceiling. At the very top, one entry flashed: **RANDY GARDNER — 264 HOURS**.

"Whoa," Noah said. "Who stayed awake for eleven straight days?"

"A **17-year-old** named **Randy Gardner**, in **San Diego**, back in **1964**, for a science-fair project," Circa said. "Still one of the longest stretches without sleep anybody's ever carefully documented."

Noah's thumb hovered over the leaderboard, a familiar itch rising — the same one that kept him up past 2 A.M. most nights. "Could I beat that?"

"Doctors genuinely do not recommend it," Circa said, flat as a patch note. "Going without sleep wrecks your mood, your focus, your memory — fast. That record isn't a flex. It's a warning label with a number on it."

Noah looked at the glowing score a second longer, then stepped back from the board on his own. "Yeah. Hard pass."

"Smart call," Circa said. "You'll spend roughly a third of your whole life asleep anyway. Might as well stop fighting it."

Noah smirked. "A third of my life, defending against a clock I can't even see. Rude."

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Animal Server Room
chapters.text:
The last corridor opened into a room full of glass tanks, each holding a flickering hologram animal.

A dolphin circled one tank, one eye open the whole time. "Dolphins, and some seals, sleep with half their brain at a time," Circa said. "One side stays awake to watch for danger, or just keep swimming."

Next tank: a giraffe, folding its long legs for a nap that lasted barely a blink. "Giraffes barely sleep at all — sometimes under two hours a day, in short naps, standing up."

Noah pointed at a tiny bat hanging upside down, perfectly still. "And this guy?"

"Some small bats sleep up to twenty hours a day. Sleepiest mammals around, easily."

In the last tank, a hologram newborn twitched constantly, eyes darting. "Newborn babies sleep **fourteen to seventeen hours a day**, almost half of it in REM sleep," Circa said.

Noah noticed one hologram glitching, wandering out of its tank with its eyes shut tight. "Is that one broken?"

"Nope. Sleepwalking," Circa said. "It happens during deep non-REM sleep, not during dreaming. Sleepwalkers usually aren't acting out anything — they're just wandering on autopilot."

Noah guided the glitching hologram gently back toward its tank. "Even fruit flies do something like this," Circa added. "Sleep's been around since basically the start of complicated life."

"Huge server room," Noah said. "Everybody's running the same patch, apparently."

chapters.heading: Level 8 (Boss): The Last Loading Screen
chapters.text:
One door remained, marked IDEAS. Behind it stood a dusty shelf holding a single glowing title: **The Interpretation of Dreams**.

"**1899**," Circa said. "**Sigmund Freud** wrote that, arguing dreams were secret wishes in disguise. Good story. Mostly not how scientists actually think it works today."

"Even old theories get outdated," Noah said.

"Most do," Circa said. "What doesn't get outdated: skip sleep for months straight, and real research links it to worse mood, worse focus, a weaker immune system. Chronic short sleep isn't a cheat code. It's a debuff you equipped yourself."

The shelf dissolved, and the static returned, pulling Noah backward through the hallway of loading bars — past the vault, the leaderboard, the clock room — until his bedroom carpet solidified under his socks again.

His phone sat face-up on the floor, battery at two percent, the little green moon fading back into an icon. One line of text sat on the lock screen: **RESPAWN SCHEDULED — SEE YOU TOMORROW NIGHT.**

Noah picked it up, plugged it into the charger, and — for the first time in one hundred and forty-two nights — set it face-down on the nightstand instead of under his pillow.

story.ending_line: Tomorrow there'd be homework, a half-finished playlist, and a whole new level to beat — but tonight, Noah actually slept.

true_facts.text: In **1953**, **Eugene Aserinsky and Nathaniel Kleitman** discovered **REM sleep** by watching a sleeping boy's eyes twitch under his closed lids.
During REM sleep your brain gets almost as busy as when you're awake, but your muscles go limp so you can't act out your dreams.
A night's sleep rolls through repeating loops about **ninety minutes** long, back and forth between quiet sleep and busy, dreaming sleep.
The deepest, quietest stage of sleep is when the body releases the most **growth hormone** — one reason growing kids need extra sleep.
A tiny part of the brain called the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, right where your eye nerves cross, works as your body's master clock.
In **2017**, **Jeffrey Hall, Michael Rosbash, and Michael Young** won the **Nobel Prize** for finding the genes that keep that body clock ticking.
The sleepy-time hormone **melatonin** was first isolated in **1958** by scientist **Aaron Lerner**'s team, taken from a tiny gland in animal brains.
Sleep helps your brain file the day's experiences into long-term memory, which is why good sleep helps you remember what you practiced.
The brain runs a nightly rinse cycle during sleep that flushes out waste, like clearing a cache.
In **1964**, a **17-year-old** named **Randy Gardner** stayed awake for about **eleven days** for a science-fair project — one of the longest stretches ever carefully documented.
Doctors don't recommend anyone try to beat a sleep record like that one, since going without sleep quickly wrecks mood, focus, and memory.
Dolphins, and some seals, sleep with only half their brain at a time, keeping one eye open to watch for danger or keep swimming.
Giraffes barely sleep at all, sometimes getting under two hours a day in brief standing naps.
Some small bats sleep up to twenty hours a day, making them some of the sleepiest mammals known.
